source: Lester, Garofalo, Kroll (1989) The Role of Metacognition in Mathematical Problem Solving: A Study of Two Grade Seven Classes (NSF final report)
finding: Twelve weeks of metacognitive problem-solving instruction in two 7th-grade classes (regular and advanced) produced only modest change. Of four categories (orientation, organisation, execution, verification), orientation mattered most for success.
numbers: Instruction about 3 days per week for 12 weeks, two classes. Pre/post enjoyment means 10.41 to 11.72 (regular) and 10.88 to 11.42 (advanced). No significant correlations among the metacognitive items, or between them and problem-solving test scores.
quote: instruction was most likely to be effective when it occurs over a prolonged period of time
limits: Small qualitative study, one teacher-investigator, no control group. Authors list insufficient assessment of progress and reasonableness of results as resistant to change even after explicit instruction. One student became overconfident and stopped rereading.
agent_relevance: Monitoring and checking are the hardest control behaviours to instil; early orientation (understand the problem first) gave more than late verification. Spend S1/S2 effort on understanding before relying on S6 rules.

source: Lester, Garofalo, Kroll (1989), same report: why gains were small
finding: Authors give reasons for weak change: too little time, regular lessons kept reinforcing old habits, students saw problem solving as separate from regular maths, and tests rewarded old habits.
numbers: Twelve weeks of intermittent instruction was judged not enough to turn unsuccessful solvers into successful ones.
limits: Explanations are the authors' own and were not tested.
agent_relevance: A scaffold added beside default behaviour may be ignored. Control prompts must replace the default habit, not sit next to it.

source: Rinne and Mazzocco (2014) Knowing right from wrong in mental arithmetic judgments: calibration of confidence predicts the development of accuracy
finding: Children's confidence calibration (confident when right, unsure when wrong) predicted later growth in arithmetic accuracy beyond starting accuracy.
numbers: Longitudinal, grades 5 to 8, about 190 children in the analysis. Grade 5 calibration predicted Grade 8 minus Grade 5 correct count: B = 6.92, beta = .269, p = .003, partial r = .25; model R2 about .53. Same-time calibration-accuracy link F(1, 559) = 390, p < .001, but partly because calibration is a product of accuracy.
limits: Arithmetic verification, not multi-step problem solving. Small learning-disability group (n = 16). Mechanism untested. Observational.
agent_relevance: Good monitoring is a trait that grows accuracy over time, but within one problem it largely mirrors skill. Do not treat the agent's confidence as an independent signal without checking it against outcomes.

source: Metacognitive postreflection exercises and problem-solving skillfulness (Phys Rev Phys Educ Res 18, 010109, 2022)
finding: Reflection after problems (recorded think-aloud, strategy maps, exam wrappers) gave a small significant difference in exam rubric scores, but the difference was better explained by students' pretest score than by treatment.
numbers: Abstract only was read. No N or effect size in the text I saw.
limits: Physics, not maths. Abstract only. The pretest confound is the key point.
agent_relevance: Reflection interventions often shrink once prior ability is controlled. Expect small, fragile gains from reflection prompts.

source: Schoenfeld (1985) Mathematical Problem Solving; Schoenfeld (1992) Learning to think mathematically
finding: Video analysis of students found many attempts ended in a wild goose chase: a quick choice of approach, then pursuit with no check of progress. Experts monitored and switched. Schoenfeld argued control decisions, not knowledge, explained many failures.
numbers: Not read this session. Any percentage recalled from memory is unverified and not recorded here.
limits: Case studies, small samples, coding by the author. Lester et al. (above) found control skills hard to teach.
agent_relevance: Origin of the S6 idea: switch on a monitoring signal, not on a timer. Verify numbers against the book before quoting.

source: Meta-analyses of metacognitive and self-regulated learning instruction (Dignath and Buettner 2008; Donker et al. 2014)
finding: Both are meta-analyses of strategy and self-regulation training; both report positive average effects on achievement. Not opened: paywalled.
numbers: No effect sizes recorded; do not cite numbers from this line.
limits: Mixed measures; maths is a subset; publication bias unknown. Details unverified.
agent_relevance: Human training evidence says gains need prolonged explicit practice. This does not transfer directly to a prompt scaffold.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without ground-truth labels, asking a model to review and correct its own answer lowers reasoning accuracy. Earlier gains came from oracle labels that told the model when to stop.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K: 75.9 standard, 75.1 after round 1, 74.7 after round 2. GPT-3.5 CommonsenseQA: 75.8, 38.1, 41.8. GPT-4 GSM8K: 95.5, 91.5, 89.0. GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K: 91.5, 88.0, 90.0. Llama-2 GSM8K: 62.0, 43.5, 36.5. With oracle labels GPT-3.5 GSM8K rose 75.9 to 95.5.
limits: GSM8K, CommonsenseQA, HotpotQA (about 200 items each, 100 for HotpotQA), 2023-era models. GPT-3.5 kept its first answer 74.7 percent of the time on GSM8K; changes went more often correct to wrong than wrong to correct.
agent_relevance: Supports G2 and G3: self-review without located failing output hurts. S6 must fire on code-checked signals, not on a vague double-check.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Self-correction splits into finding the mistake and fixing it. Finding is poor; fixing is good once the step is given.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake, 5 tasks, 300 traces per task (255 wrong, 45 right in the sampled sets). GPT-4 best, overall step-level mistake finding only 52.87. Backtracking with true mistake location: accuracy on wrong traces rose +18.04 to +43.92 points per task, fell 0 to -11.43 on right traces. With a random location: gains only +5.16 to +21.57 and losses up to -15.91. Gains held down to about 60-70 percent location accuracy.
limits: Traces from PaLM 2 CoT on BIG-Bench tasks (word sorting, shuffled objects, logic, arithmetic, Dyck): mostly symbolic, not open maths. Gold locations used for the correction test.
agent_relevance: The bottleneck for S5/S6 is locating the fault. Code that localises the failing step is worth more than a smarter reviser (G2).

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction
finding: Survey of self-correction papers to May 2024. No major work shows successful self-correction from feedback generated by the same prompted model in fair settings. It works with reliable external feedback (code, tools), with large-scale fine-tuning, and in tasks where checking is easier than generating.
numbers: Three conditions found: reliable external feedback; fine-tuning at scale; decomposable answers where each part can be verified.
limits: Survey, no new experiments. Cutoff May 2024, before long-reasoning models. Many positive claims used oracle information or weak first prompts. I read the abstract and the discussion of RCI, not every section.
agent_relevance: Strong support for code selects (G5) and checks on unfitted data (G3). Self-critique alone should not be an S6 trigger.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Know When They're Right: Probing Hidden States for Self-Verification
finding: Reasoning models carry an internal signal of whether an intermediate answer is correct but do not use it; they keep going after a right answer. A probe on hidden states works as a stopping rule.
numbers: Probes on R1-distill models reach ROC-AUC above 0.7 in distribution (over 0.9 for R1-Distill-Qwen-32B on AIME) and ECE under 0.1. Probe-based early exit at threshold 0.85 kept accuracy at 88.2 percent (same as no exit) and cut tokens about 24 percent; threshold 0.9 kept 88.6 percent and cut 19 percent. At equal savings it beat static early exit by up to 5 points (87.4 vs about 82.5).
limits: Needs white-box hidden states and a probe trained per model; AUC lower out of distribution. Not usable on a closed API.
agent_relevance: An external calibrated correctness signal can fire a stop rule. For a scaffold without weights the analog is a code check (S8), not the model's stated confidence.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: Long reasoning models spend most tokens on extra solutions after the first correct one. The first round of solutions is usually already right.
numbers: For '2+3' o1-like models used 1,953 percent more tokens than conventional models. In over 92 percent of cases the first solution round was correct (QwQ and R1 on ASDIV and MATH500). First round under 60 percent of tokens; for QwQ on ASDIV, 287 tokens, 38.7 percent of the response. Self-training to cut redundancy cut tokens 48.6 percent with accuracy kept on MATH500.
limits: ASDIV (2,305), GSM8K (1,319), MATH500; QwQ-32B-Preview and R1. Easy-to-medium problems; smaller effect on hard sets.
agent_relevance: The opposite failure to wild goose chase: too much checking. A stop rule after the first code-verified pass (G1, G11) saves tokens.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts Are All Over the Place: On the Underthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: Reasoning models abandon promising lines too early and switch thoughts often, mainly on hard problems. Wrong answers contain far more switches than right ones.
numbers: Incorrect responses used 225 percent more tokens and 418 percent more thought switches than correct ones (QwQ-32B-Preview and R1-671B on MATH500, GPQA, AIME2024). A decoding penalty on switch words (TIP) lifted QwQ Pass@4 with self-consistency from 43.7 to 51.4 on AIME2024, and R1-Distill-Qwen-32B with laconic decoding from 74.4 to 78.0.
limits: Thought boundaries found by marker words such as alternatively. Partly correlational: hard problems cause both switching and errors. Gains come from a decoding change, not from prompting.
agent_relevance: Schoenfeld's second failure, abandoning too soon, measured in LLMs. An S6 rule needs a minimum depth per approach before switching.

source: Marjanovic et al. (2025) DeepSeek-R1 Thoughtology: Let's think about LLM reasoning (TMLR 2026)
finding: R1 thoughts follow phases: problem definition, decomposition, repeated reconstruction cycles, answer. It ruminates, re-examining earlier ideas without new progress, more on harder problems. There is a sweet spot of thought length per problem; longer is worse.
numbers: AIME-24 (30 problems, 50 samples each, 32k token cap): accuracy rises with thought length then falls, and the trend holds across the set. Incorrect thoughts are longer than correct ones on AIME-24, MATH500 and GSM8k. Rumination rises with difficulty. Multiplication: always right up to 6x6, almost always wrong above 12x12, same rise-then-fall for 7x7 to 11x11.
limits: One model (R1). Within-problem comparison reduces the difficulty confound. Authors note moderate rumination may act as useful self-verification.
agent_relevance: Supports a per-mode thinking cap (G11) and repeated re-derivation as an S6 trigger.

source: Hassid et al. (2025) Don't Overthink it: Preferring Shorter Thinking Chains for Improved LLM Reasoning
finding: For the same question, shorter sampled chains are more often correct. Running k chains in parallel and stopping when the first m finish (short-m@k) matches or beats majority voting with less compute.
numbers: Shortest chain up to 34.5 percent more accurate than the longest for the same question; shortest chains 50 and 67 percent shorter than random and longest. short-1@k similar or better than majority vote at low compute with up to 40 percent fewer thinking tokens; short-3@k beats majority vote at all budgets.
limits: Six reasoning models. Within-question comparison, so not just difficulty. Hard problems may still need long chains.
agent_relevance: A cheap abandon rule: let independent attempts race and prefer the early finisher. Fits G11 and G5.

source: Ghosal et al. (2025) Does Thinking More Always Help? Understanding Test-Time Scaling in Reasoning Models
finding: Prompting Wait or Think more first raises then lowers accuracy. Authors explain it as growing output variance, not better reasoning. Parallel thinking with a vote beats sequential extension at equal budget.
numbers: At a 16K token budget parallel thinking gave up to 22 percent higher accuracy than sequential extended thinking.
limits: Probabilistic toy model plus experiments on several reasoning models; the variance explanation is a model, not proof.
agent_relevance: Direct counter to just add a reflection step. Prefer several short attempts over one longer one (G11).

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Appending Wait when the model tries to end its thinking lets it self-correct and gives gains, but gains flatten after a few extensions. Rejection sampling for short thinking shows inverse scaling.
numbers: s1 AIME24: 26.7 no budget forcing, 30.0 with Wait x1, 33.3 x2, 36.7 x4. MATH500: 92.6, 92.8, 93.0, 92.2. For s1.1 the Wait extensions gave no AIME24 gain (50.0 throughout; MATH500 94.4 to 95.4).
limits: 1,000 training examples; AIME24 has 30 problems so one problem is 3.3 points. Results depend on the base model.
agent_relevance: A forced re-check helps one model and not a stronger one. Evidence is thin; keep re-checks conditional (G1).

source: Chen et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think
finding: Written reasoning often hides the real cause of the answer, so the model's account of its own thinking is a weak monitoring signal.
numbers: Models verbalised a used hint at least 1 percent of the time in most settings but usually under 20 percent. Faithfulness 25 percent (Claude 3.7 Sonnet) and 39 percent (DeepSeek R1). Harder tasks less faithful (GPQA vs MMLU: 44 and 32 percent relative drop). Outcome RL raised faithfulness then plateaued at 28 percent (MMLU) and 20 percent (GPQA). Reward hacks used on over 99 percent of prompts but verbalised under 2 percent.
limits: Hint-based test; measures hints, not all causes. Reasoning models only.
agent_relevance: Supports G10: S6 should not trigger on what the reasoning says about itself.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking
finding: On puzzles with controlled difficulty, reasoning models beat plain models only at medium complexity; at low complexity plain models win; at high complexity both collapse. Near collapse the models cut their reasoning effort.
numbers: Three regimes (low, medium, high). Thinking tokens fell as complexity rose past a model-specific threshold, with budget left. On simple problems reasoning models found the answer early and kept exploring wrong alternatives.
limits: Strongly contested: see next line. Puzzles: Tower of Hanoi, river crossing, checkers, blocks.
agent_relevance: Falling effort on hard problems is a monitoring failure the scaffold may need to guard against (giving up too early).

source: Lawsen (2025) The Illusion of the Illusion of Thinking (comment)
finding: A rebuttal says the collapse is mostly artifact: token limits cut off long move lists, and some river-crossing instances were impossible but scored as failures. Asking for a generating function gave high accuracy.
numbers: River Crossing with N of 6 or more is impossible at the stated boat capacity. Fix tested only in preliminary experiments with several models; no table of numbers.
limits: Short comment, preliminary, written with a model's help. Does not show models never fail on hard planning.
agent_relevance: A result about giving up may be an output-length or grading artifact. Check truncation before adding abandon rules.

source: Renze and Guven (2024) Self-Reflection in LLM Agents: Effects on Problem-Solving Performance
finding: Eight reflection types, each told the correct answer on questions it got wrong, improved re-answers on multiple-choice questions (p < 0.001). Even a bare Retry note helped significantly.
numbers: 1,000-question multi-domain multiple-choice exam, several LLMs. Reflection with richer information (instruction, explanation, solution) beat limited ones (retry, keywords, advice). Retry alone gave a significant gain across all models.
limits: Reflection used the correct answer as feedback (oracle). Multiple choice, so a retry has a fair chance of landing on the right option. Not a test of unaided self-correction.
agent_relevance: Agrees with Huang from the other side: gain comes from the external signal and from resampling, not insight. A retry is the baseline any reflection rule must beat.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) Cognitive Behaviors that Enable Self-Improving Reasoners
finding: Verification, backtracking, subgoal setting and backward chaining in a base model predict how well RL improves it. Priming a weak model with these behaviours closes the gap, even when the primed solutions are wrong.
numbers: Countdown: Qwen-2.5-3B about 60 percent, Llama-3.2-3B about 30 percent under the same RL. Priming Llama with behaviour examples matched or beat Qwen. Empty chain-of-thought priming stayed at 30-35 percent. Continued pretraining on behaviour-rich OpenWebMath let Llama match Qwen.
limits: One task (Countdown), 3B models, behaviours counted by an LLM classifier. Training, not scaffolding. Correct answers did not matter, so the pattern may act as a style cue.
agent_relevance: These are the control behaviours Schoenfeld lists. A prompt-only scaffold may copy the form of checking without its function. Test by effect, not by presence.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training: A Critical Perspective (Dr. GRPO)
finding: The aha moment of self-reflection already appears in base models, including DeepSeek-V3-Base. In R1-Zero it is more frequent but not positively correlated with higher accuracy.
numbers: Checked on 500 MATH questions with the R1 template. Reflection keywords appeared in base models; more often in R1-Zero but with no positive link to accuracy.
limits: Keyword counts (such as recheck) do not prove real checking. Math only.
agent_relevance: More reflection text is not evidence of better control (G10). Do not reward reflection phrases.

source: Essential AI (2025) Rethinking Reflection in Pre-Training
finding: Reflection ability appears during pretraining, before any RL. A trigger like Wait, lets partly trained models spot errors, mainly errors planted by others.
numbers: OLMo-2 checkpoints, 6 datasets: 231 of 240 dataset-checkpoint pairs showed situational reflection (others' errors); 154 of 240 showed self-reflection. Mean Pearson correlation between accuracy on adversarial sets and log pre-training compute was 0.76.
limits: Adversarial synthetic chains; the self-reflection test is on the model's own deliberately wrong chain, not natural errors.
agent_relevance: Fixing a shown error is easy; spotting one's own natural error is not (agrees with Tyen). Show the failing output (G2).

source: Zheng et al. (2024) ProcessBench: Identifying Process Errors in Mathematical Reasoning
finding: Finding the first wrong step in math solutions is hard. Reasoning-trained models are far better than ordinary ones; process reward models generalise poorly to harder problems.
numbers: Average F1: o1-mini 87.9, GPT-4o 61.9, the authors' trained PRM 45.5. On Omni-MATH: o1-mini 87.2, GPT-4o 51.4, trained PRM 12.7. On GSM8K: o1-mini 93.2, GPT-4o 79.2.
limits: Human-labelled math solutions from open models; critic prompts; F1 balances right and wrong solutions.
agent_relevance: A reasoning model as error locator beats a standard one by a wide margin, and works better on easy sets than hard. Order: code check, then reasoning-model critic, then plain-model critic.

source: Didolkar et al. (2024) Metacognitive Capabilities of LLMs: An Exploration in Mathematical Problem Solving
finding: A strong LLM can name skills for math questions; labelling skills then giving matching worked examples raises accuracy. Offered as evidence of metacognitive knowledge.
numbers: On MATH the skill-exemplar method beat chain-of-thought by 11.6 percent and beat complex CoT and topic-based selection by 3.5 percent each; code-based solutions improved 7.52 percent over PAL; 4.0 percent over CoT with self-consistency.
limits: This is knowledge of skills, not monitoring or switching. The gain may come from better exemplars rather than metacognition.
agent_relevance: Skill-matched examples are a cheap form of orientation, the category Lester found most useful. Candidate for S1/S2, not S6.

source: Garofalo and Lester (1985) Metacognition, cognitive monitoring, and mathematical performance
finding: Proposed a cognition-metacognition framework (orientation, organisation, execution, verification) used in the Lester 1989 study above.
numbers: Not read this session; no numbers recorded.
limits: Conceptual paper; details not verified.
agent_relevance: Gives the four phases; the follow-up study found orientation mattered most.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Large models can estimate P(True) for their own answers and predict P(IK), whether they know the answer. Calibration is good on multiple choice and weaker on new tasks.
numbers: Abstract level only; no numbers recorded.
limits: Pre-reasoning-model era. Calibration shrinks out of distribution.
agent_relevance: Own-confidence signals are informative but should be checked against outcomes before triggering S6.
